summary: Reviewed the dvpwa 'sqli' aiohttp application: DAO layer (SQL access), views/routes (HTTP handlers), auth/session utilities, middlewares, app factory, config and Jinja2 templates. The application is riddled with serious, reachable vulnerabilities: an unauthenticated SQL injection in student creation, global disabling of template auto-escaping leading to stored XSS, disabled CSRF protection, MD5 password hashing, session cookies without HttpOnly, and state-changing endpoints with no authentication/authorization. Overall risk is critical: an unauthenticated remote attacker can inject SQL, store XSS, and manipulate application data. Static-only review; runtime behaviour and deployment hardening were not observed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create via string-formatted INSERT
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python %-formatting of the raw 'name' value instead of a parameterized query. The name flows directly from unauthenticated user input: views.students (sqli/views.py:54-57) reads data['name'] from a POST to /students/ and passes it to Student.create with no validation (STUDENT_SCHEMA is never applied) and no login check. CSRF protection is also disabled, so any remote, unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary SQL. Because psycopg allows stacked/UNION queries and the only quoting is a naive single-quote wrapper, the attacker can read/modify any table (e.g. dump users.pwd_hash) or corrupt data.
findings.evidence:
q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  # sqli/dao/student.py:42-43
await cur.execute(q)  # no params
Source: views.students -> data = await request.post(); await Student.create(conn, data['name'])  # sqli/views.py:55-57
Example payload for name: ') ; DROP TABLE marks; -- or ')||(SELECT pwd_hash FROM users)||('
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute('INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)', {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/f-string formatting of user input. Additionally validate name with STUDENT_SCHEMA and require authentication/CSRF on the handler.

findings.title: Stored XSS via globally disabled Jinja2 auto-escaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so every template variable is rendered as raw HTML unless an explicit '| e' filter is present. Many user-controlled values are rendered without escaping: course review_text and course.title/description in course.jinja2 (lines 14-15, 22), and student name in students.jinja2 (line 16). Reviews can be created by any unauthenticated user (views.review, sqli/views.py:111-131) and student names are attacker-controlled (views.students). An attacker submits a review/name containing <script>... which executes in the browser of every visitor to the course/student page (stored XSS). Combined with HttpOnly being disabled on the session cookie, this allows session hijacking.
findings.evidence:
setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)  # sqli/app.py:35
course.jinja2:22 -> {{ review.review_text }} (no |e); students.jinja2:16 -> {{ name }} (no |e)
Sink reached by: views.review POST -> Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text)  # sqli/views.py:129
findings.recommendation: Enable auto-escaping: setup_jinja(..., autoescape=True) (aiohttp_jinja2 passes this to Jinja2's Environment). Escape by default and use the |safe filter only for trusted, pre-sanitized HTML.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
findings.description: The csrf_middleware (defined in sqli/middlewares.py:25-38 and would validate the _csrf_token against the session) is commented out of the middleware chain. As a result none of the POST handlers (create student, create course, submit review, evaluate/grade a student, logout) verify the CSRF token even though templates emit it. Any website can forge cross-site POSTs on behalf of a logged-in user/admin, e.g. grading students or creating data, and unauthenticated POSTs (student/review creation) are likewise forgeable. This also removes the only mitigation that would blunt cross-site exploitation of the SQLi and XSS issues above.
findings.evidence:
middlewares=[
    session_middleware,
    # csrf_middleware,   <-- disabled
    error_middleware,
]  # sqli/app.py:25-29
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and verify every state-changing POST carries a valid per-session token. Also set SameSite on the session cookie as defense in depth.

findings.title: Missing authentication/authorization on state-changing endpoints (incl. admin grading)
findings.description: The @authorize decorator exists (sqli/utils/auth.py:12-23) but is applied only to logout. All other handlers perform privileged actions with no auth check. evaluate() creates student marks (a grading action the UI only exposes to admins via 'auth_user.is_admin' in course.jinja2:41) yet the handler has no @authorize(ensure_admin=True) and no session check, so any anonymous user can POST grades. The same missing-authorization flaw applies to students() creating students (views.py:51-60), courses() creating courses (views.py:83-93), and review() creating reviews (views.py:111-131). Server-side access control is entirely absent; UI-level is_admin checks provide no protection.
findings.evidence:
async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  # sqli/views.py:135-152, no @authorize
Contrast: UI gates this behind {% if auth_user.is_admin %} in course.jinja2:41
Only logout uses @authorize()  # sqli/views.py:156
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize() to all authenticated actions and @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to admin-only ones (e.g. evaluate). Enforce access control server-side at a trusted layer; do not rely on template conditionals.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash against md5(password). Passwords are stored as fast, unsalted MD5 digests, which are trivially brute-forced/rainbow-tabled. If the users table is exposed (e.g. via the SQL injection above, which can read pwd_hash), attacker can recover plaintext passwords almost instantly. MD5 is also unsuitable because it is not memory-hard and lacks per-user salt.
findings.evidence:
from hashlib import md5
...
def check_password(self, password): return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  # sqli/dao/user.py:1,40-41
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted password hash such as Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt (e.g. the 'argon2-cffi' or 'bcrypt' library). Migrate existing hashes on next login. Use constant-time comparison.

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS from disabled auto-escaping, an attacker's injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier, enabling full session hijacking. No Secure or SameSite attributes are configured either.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (default is True) and set secure=True and samesite='Lax'/'Strict' on the session storage so the cookie cannot be read by scripts or sent cross-site over plaintext.

findings.title: aiohttp application started with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is created with debug=True unconditionally. Debug mode enables verbose diagnostics and more permissive behaviour that can leak internal information and should never be on in production. The value is hard-coded rather than driven by configuration/environment.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False. Ensure production deployments run with debug disabled.

findings.title: Hard-coded database credentials in committed config
findings.description: The committed configuration contains a static database username and password (postgres/postgres). This is the default config path used by the app factory (default_config='./config/dev.yaml' in sqli/app.py:18). Committing credentials, even weak/default ones, encourages their reuse in real deployments and exposes them to anyone with repo access.
findings.evidence:
db:
  user: postgres
  password: postgres  # config/dev.yaml:2-3
findings.recommendation: Load secrets from environment variables or a secrets manager; keep only non-secret defaults in the repo and use strong, unique credentials per environment.
